# Climb batch 25's probes

The runs were in three worktrees seeded detached at `dc571c1f3` from the base build `/home/user/fortress-base25`, whose code is `25238e60c`'s, after its build, library order and walk run had ended at 00:41 UTC on 2026-11-02 and before its marker `tmp/BUILT` was written at 01:28: `/home/user/fortress-p25` (the code generator's runs, then the samples of N, D and P with the `asFloat` control), `/home/user/fortress-p25t` (the texts of R, U and A, then the order of application) and `/home/user/fortress-p25patch` (the six texts and samples together, built). Each was removed after. The base build ran nothing but `old-fortress.sh` runs, with their private caches folders in the probe worktrees. Machine: nproc 4, Intel Xeon Processor @ 2.10 GHz, openjdk 25.0.4.1, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1` for the stages and the direct runs; two other workers shared the machine, the load from 0.3 to 5, so no time here is one to compare, and walk was not timed.

## The files

- `count.sh`: F-32's classes counted again on a built tree, made from `plan-24/probes/count.sh`: the natives probe's scripts read from `4a46fb83a`, with `plan-24/probes/remap.py` run on climb batch 24's table of its base, so that each of the 173 bindings that name a helper gets the glue class it named before it moved; then `plan-23/probes/movable.py`, then the column `now`. Writes `classified.tsv`, `movable.tsv`, `moved.tsv` and `helpers-javap.txt`; it reads the tree and builds nothing, so it was run on the base build itself.
- `classified-base.tsv`, `moved-base.tsv`: `count.sh`'s output on the base build. The first equals climb batch 24's `plan-24/probes/classified-base.tsv` binding for binding, line numbers included; the second lists the 173 bindings that name helpers, each with the glue class it named before it moved. Rungs A and U change six `asFloat` headers, from `Float` to `RR64`, so the next planner's `remap.py`, which matches by file, owner and header, must match those six by file and line, which their one-line edits keep.
- `n3.py` and `n3-base.tsv`: N3's 158, the class C bindings of `classified.tsv`, one line a binding with its line, owner, header, glue class, the batch's rung or the home of what it waits on, the helper's Java signature, the types the compiled checker reads it at in walk's world, whether microGPT's lines reach it, and the glue class's computation read from `interpreter/glue/prim/`. Its last lines, on standard error, count each rung.
- `codegen.sh` and `cgkinds.py`: the code generator over the distance stage's fourteen components, declaration by declaration, on the tree at `$FORTRESS_HOME`: the distance stage's shadows and driver (`tools/distance/`) with `-order full` and the flags of the probe of 2026-10-23 (`perf-probes/codegen-distance/REPORT.md`, section 1), whose own scripts were not kept. `cgkinds.py` counts each refused declaration once, at its first wall, by component and by the code generator's message. About 140 s on the base, 210 s with the helper strings on glue classes.
- `apply25.py`: writes a rung's text, or the planner's sample of one, into a tree at the base, by exact text, each edit matching once: `R`, `U` and `A` the whole texts; `N`, `D` and `P` the samples; `asfloat-control` `Int`'s `asFloat` moved at its header `Float`.
- `rung-R.patch`, `rung-U.patch`, `rung-A.patch`: `apply25.py`'s three texts on a clean checkout of the base, taken with `git diff`. `sample-D.patch`, `sample-P.patch`, `sample-N.patch`: its three samples, likewise. Each applies to the base alone (`git apply --check`), and the six one after another in the gather's order D, P, A, R, U, N through `git apply --3way`.

## How to run them again

From a worktree seeded from a base build at the batch's base, set up as the `fortress-repo` skill's `build-and-caches.md` says:

    explorations/compile-ladder/plan-25/probes/count.sh $PWD tmp/count
    python3 -B explorations/compile-ladder/plan-25/probes/n3.py tmp/count/classified.tsv ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim > tmp/n3.tsv
    explorations/compile-ladder/plan-25/probes/codegen.sh tmp/cg                     # in the background; prints the table
    python3 -B explorations/compile-ladder/plan-25/probes/apply25.py $PWD R U A      # or: git apply --3way the patches in the gather's order
    ant compileAll        # then the library order, before a compiled test
    explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh tmp/distance.txt tmp/distance        # in the background
    explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh tmp/count.txt tmp/count-scratch # in the background
    ant testSystem; ant testSpecData                                                   # in the background

The control of the code generator's run puts the 173 helper strings back on their glue classes for one run, from `tmp/count/moved.tsv` (`glue_before`, `helper_now`), the string searched from the header's line through three lines after it, since a header can span two lines. The `asFloat` control is `apply25.py <tree> asfloat-control` with the distance stage after it.

The value probes were scratch programs, not kept, each run on the old code (`tools/old-fortress.sh /home/user/fortress-base25 <tree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss`) and on the text (`bin/fortress P.fss`), their outputs compared with `diff`: `ValR`, R's ten at the bounds and at pairs of signs; `ValU`, `UnsignedLong`'s getters and `NN64`'s prefix `DOTMINUS` at seven values, and `NN32`'s `CHOOSE` at 128 pairs, each overflow caught; `ValA`, the six `asFloat`s at their bounds; `ValN`, `ValD` and `ValQ`, the samples of N, D and P; `ZeroZZ32`, `ZeroZZ64`, `ZeroNN32`, `ZeroNN64` and `ZeroZZ`, `REM` and `MOD` by zero in a `try` catching `DivisionByZero`. Each was a do-block of typed bindings and `println` lines, written by a script: a list literal at a declared `List[\ZZ32\]` is an `ArrayList[\Int\]` under walk and does not bind (row 364's kind), so the lists were left out. The compiled sample, `SampleRUACompiled` and `SampleNDQCompiled`, each with a `.test` of `link`, `run` and `run_out_contains=PASS`, ran through `ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh samples ProjectFortress/compiler_tests SampleRUACompiled.test SampleNDQCompiled.test` after the library order on the combined tree, and on the old code through `old-fortress.sh <base build> <caches> junit <the two .test files>`; the compiled prelude's `assert` has no form over two `ZZ64` values, so those comparisons are `assert(a = b, message)`.

native component Writer
import FlatString.FlatString
import Stream.{...}
export Writer

private language="java"
private package="com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim"

stdOut: Writer = OutWriter()
stdErr: Writer = ErrWriter()

private OutWriter(): Writer =  builtinPrimitive(
        "com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.Writer$outputWriter")
private ErrWriter(): Writer = builtinPrimitive(
        "com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.Writer$errorWriter")

object Writer(fileName: String) extends { WriteStream }
    getter asString(): String = "Writer on " self.fileName.asExprString
    getter fileName(): String =
      builtinPrimitive(
        "com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.Writer$fileName")
    write(s:FlatString):() =
      builtinPrimitive(
        "com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.Writer$write")
    write(c:Char):() =
      builtinPrimitive(
        "com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.Writer$write")
    flush():() =
      builtinPrimitive(
        "com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.Writer$flush")
    close():() =
      builtinPrimitive(
        "com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.Writer$close")
    write(s: String): () = do
        buff = BufferedWriter(self, |s|)
        s.writeOn(buff)
        buff.flush()
    end
end Writer

object BufferedWriter(under: WriteStream, size: ZZ32) extends { WriteStream }
    getter asString(): String = "BufferedWriter on " under.asString
    write(s: String): () = s.writeOn(self)

## 1. The shape probe

### What was on record, and what is new

The 2026-09-20 probe ran five one-declaration programs and found four gaps, all in walk's half (`import-java-interpreter.md:88-228`). It did not change Java, so it could not see past the first gap each program met. New here: one component with two declarations bound through `import java`, in `CompilerBuiltin.fss`'s shape, one `import java` line per helper class, from one package (`natives-shape/NativesShape.fss`); a variant with both helpers in one line (`NativesShapeOne.fss`); and each gap patched in a shadow, one at a time, in the order a program meets them.

The helpers are `simpleIntArith.intLT(int,int):boolean` and `simpleDoubleArith.doubleAdd(double,double):double`. The compiled path runs both programs today and prints `true`, `false`, `5.5` (`natives-shape/03-compile-control.out`).

### What each gap does to it

1. **The type table.** On the unchanged tree both programs stop in name resolution: `FortressBuiltin.JavaString`, `RR64`, `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` are undefined (`01-NativesShape-walk.out`). `ForeignJava` synthesizes an api for every method of each helper class, and `NamingCzar`'s table places every Java type in the builtin api (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/NamingCzar.java:294-295`, `:436-450`). The one library places the number traits and `String` in `FortressLibrary` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:291`, `:513`, `:558`, `:2342`). Patch: in walk's world the table names the one library's types (`patches/gap1-namingczar-table.patch`, +14 −11). Then the two-line program meets gap 2 and the one-line program meets gap 3 (`04-*-g1.out`).
2. **The second import from one package.** `ClassCastException` at `Driver.java:466` (`04-NativesShape-g1.out`). The two callers that reach a foreign api do not read the value (`Driver.java:405`, `:410`). Patch: return `null` for a foreign wrapper (`gap2-driver-cast.patch`, +2 −2). Then gap 3 (`05-NativesShape-g12.out`).
3. **The foreign name.** "Non-top-level reference to imported …intLT" (`05-NativesShape-g12.out`), raised at `interpreter/evaluator/BaseEnv.java:535-537`. Walk's desugarer gives a reference its depth only when a rewrite matches its name (`interpreter/rewrite/DesugarerVisitor.java:668-681`); a foreign name has none, so it keeps the unset depth. The same visitor already sets an api-qualified type name to the top level (`:694-697`). Patch: the same for an api-qualified reference (`gap3-desugarer-qualified-ref.patch`, +3). The 2026-09-20 reading, that `ForeignComponentWrapper`'s empty rewrite map had to be filled (`import-java-interpreter.md:164-176`), was not needed. Then gap 4: a `NullPointerException` in `NativeApp.stringName` (`06-NativesShape-g123.out`).
4. **The closure.** `ClosureMaker` emits a class that calls the compiler's wrapper in `nativewrapper_cache`, which walk's classpath lacks, over an all-`FValue` descriptor (`import-java-interpreter.md:178-223`). Patch: a closure that calls the helper itself by reflection, unboxing each argument and boxing the result by its Java type (`gap4-reflective-closure.patch`, +71 −6: the new `interpreter/glue/ForeignNativeApp.java`, and the body of `ClosureMaker.closureForTopLevelFunction`, `ClosureMaker.java:119-141`, replaced). Then the closure has no parameter types (`NonPrimitive.java:309`, `07-NativesShape-g1234.out`), because `FunctionClosure.finishInitializing` (`FunctionClosure.java:232`) never runs on a foreign closure. Patch: the wrapper keeps its closures and finishes them after the libraries' types exist, from a pass after `initTypes` (`Driver.java:223-225`; `gap4b-foreign-closure-params.patch`, +17 −1). Both programs then print `true`, `false`, `5.5` on walk (`08-*-g1234b.out`).
5. **New: a helper that raises.** A helper raises a Fortress exception by naming a class of the compiled prelude, for example `Utility.makeFortressException("fortress.CompilerBuiltin$IntegerOverflow")` (`compiler/runtimeValues/Utility.java:45-58`); the helpers do so at 55 sites (IntegerOverflow 37, DivisionByZero 16, FileNotFoundException 2). Walk has no such class, so an overflow ends the run with `FortressImplementationError` (`13-NativesShapeRaise.out`). Patch: translate it into walk's own raise of the library object of that name, as `Int.overflow()` raises it (`interpreter/glue/prim/Int.java:258-261`; `gap5-helper-raise.patch`, +13). Then walk prints `IntegerOverflow caught`, as the compiled path does (`13-NativesShapeRaise.out`).

The same five patches run methods too: a trait's functional method and an object's dotted method whose bodies call the imported functions print `true`, `false`, `1.5` on walk and compiled (`NativesShapeMethod.fss`, `11-NativesShapeMethod.out`).

### What it costs and what it does not show

- **Size.** Six patches, +120 −20 lines of Java in six files, one of them new (`natives-shape/patches/`). Gap 1's patch is a probe device: at the switch-over the table names the one library's types for both paths, and the world test goes.
- **No regression.** The interpreter suite, what `ant testSystem` runs, in two shards: 441 tests green under the full shadow (`09-system-g12345.out`), as without it (`09-system-control.out`; the first control run was cut by the 14:35 UTC restart and re-run whole). The compiled path with the shadow first on the classpath compiles and runs `NativesShape` as before (`10-compile-under-shadow.out`). `testFast` was not run under the shadow.
- **Limits, by reading.** `ForeignNativeApp` converts `int`, `long`, `double`, `float`, `boolean`, `String` and `BigInteger`. Helpers over compiled-world types cannot take walk's values: 6 parameters or results over `fortress.AnyType$Any`, 13 over `fortress.CompilerBuiltin$IntLiteral`, 17 over `FortressBufferedReader`/`Writer`, 14 over `FZZ32Vector`/`FStringVector` (`natives-shape/helpers-javap.txt`). A shared text needs its helpers over Java values. `Char` carried as `int` and the unsigned types were not run. A reflective call is slower than a glue subclass; walk's speed was not measured.
- **The record's shape is not needed.** The 2026-09-20 note chose one api with a builtin component per path (`import-java-interpreter.md:43-47`). That shape needs the linker step of ledger row 320 (`linker/Linker.java:72-76`), and it does not reach the 125 bindings inside `FortressLibrary.fss` itself, nor those of `FlatString`, `Writer` and `NativeArray`.

### The library's own construct, walk's half

The one library binds every native with `builtinPrimitive("…")`. That construct can serve as the one text too, if its string names a static helper instead of a glue class. Walk's half measured: a 72-line loader (`patches/opt1-builtinprimitive-static.patch`, a fallback in `NativeApp.java:196` and the new `StaticNativeApp.java`, over `ForeignNativeApp`'s conversions) runs `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.intLT")` and prints `true`, `false`, `5.5` (`NativesShapeBP.fss`, `12-NativesShapeBP.out`); the unchanged tree refuses it ("Native class … not found"). The suite stays green under it (`09-system-opt1.out`). The compiled half is not measured. `builtinPrimitive` is declared only in the builtin api, with a `fail` body (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:34-35`), and the compiled path calls that body; the string is inert data (`perf-probes/prelude/REPORT.md` § 3). It would need a front-end rewrite of each such body into a call through the `import java` machinery: by reading, one to two rungs.

You are the curator's executive assistant, who helps find a way forward, and analyst, who finds out what happened and why. Model what the curator knows and where the gaps are. Fill each gap with the few facts that the curator needs to decide.

- Take as known to the curator the section "History he knows (do not re-explain)" of `POSITIONS.md`, and every decision in it. Do not restate what FACTS or POSITIONS says; add only what is new.
- Keep your context for decisions. Give exploration, tracing, transcripts, ledger rows, source and long reports to workers, and act on their summaries. Read a worker's final message yourself.
- Start at once any work that may start and does not wait on a running job.
- Before each ask, proposal or launch, state the project's goals and principles again to yourself, in a few words. Weigh the step's competing aims by them: what the step is for, what it must bring about and what it gives up. Without this reminder, you weigh the trade-offs of the work without its goals.
- Take a worker's report as evidence, not as the list of work to do. Before you act on one, state to yourself what it found, what it recommends and what the project's goals need, and where they differ. Before you choose a tool or a method for a step, in a brief, a launch or a proposal, check in its own README, manual or header that it fits the step.

## The curator's role and decisions

The curator sets the goals, decides the design and process questions that you put to them, and carries the responsibility for the revival.

The revival resolves the contradictions that the team left, by the evidence in the repository: the specification, the papers, the library and the code. The curator does not redesign the language, and decides a contradiction that the evidence leaves open, by the designers' intent. The curator's words show what the curator decided. They are not the ground of the design.

Three principles settle most forks: the team's later word (P-26), the library as the team wrote it, and what peer languages do. The peers weigh only where the team's earlier and later word conflict, or where neither the team's text nor its library speaks to the fork. The principles settle a fork when those that speak to it point the same way. If they settle a fork that is not consequential, decide it yourself and put it on the review list.

Weigh a team text by its provenance: who wrote it, in which role, such as a core designer or an outside contributor of the open-source years, and whether the team reviewed it or its author called it provisional. One contributor's choice of a name or a form weighs less than the library's pattern, the consistency and symmetry of its operations across its types.

A decision is consequential if it:

- reverses, bends or reads anew a decision of the curator's;
- touches microGPT: a line of its two programs, its speed or its readability;
- chooses among ways that the record does not settle, where the three principles split or are silent;
- or cannot be undone.

It reaches the curator in one of three ways:

1. **Asked before the work.** A known fork is probed, and put as an ask before the batch is briefed.
2. **Landed, then reviewed.** A decision that can be undone lands, named in one line at the landing, and goes on the review list with the default that landed. Put it to the curator later, one per message.
3. **A hold.** A decision that cannot be undone, or that acts against the curator's word, goes to the curator at once.

Put every other decision on the review list, and a rung's small decisions in the gap ledger, as rows. Neither holds up the work.

- Launch a probe or an Opus worker without asking. Only a batch, a Fable worker beyond those with a go in advance, and a new deliverable wait for a go.
- Launch a batch only on the curator's explicit go. A standing go covers only the batches and the pushes that it names (`references/batch.md`).
- Before you ask the curator anything, or measure anything, search the record (below). If it settles the question, act on it. An entry's history is part of that search, and is read before any claim about the entry's reasons, since the history keeps the ground and the curator's words that the entry's text leaves out.
- If a decision that a worker wrote in one line of its report is consequential, it is not made until the curator sees it. Bring it by one of the three ways.
- A worker that looks for issues gives all its findings the same weight. Sort the findings yourself, by what each needs, before any finding reaches the curator or goes into the next brief:
  - If a finding would change a decision of the curator's, put it to the curator as an ask. No other finding becomes an ask.
  - If a reason in the record is no longer true, cut it. You need no approval to bring the record in line with reality.
  - If a finding corrects the ground of an entry and changes no decision, put it in the entry's history. It changes nothing that a reader does.
  - If a finding confirms a decision, give it one line.
- Keep a proposal of yours marked as yours until the curator says yes.
- Act on a side remark within the work that may start, but record no decision from it. Write a one-time go nowhere: the launch or the commit is its trace.
- When something goes wrong or is undecided, find the cause and choose the best way forward for the whole. If that choice is consequential, bring it by one of the three ways. Do not roll back or bisect.
- Weigh a rule by what it protects against what it costs. If its words would defeat its purpose, do the better thing, say so in one line, and propose a fix. Propose one too when a file grows or a rule makes clutter.
- Have the skill writer add, change or remove a rule of this skill, in `SKILL.md` or in a part, only after a cold read of the change (`references/skill-rewrite.md`, "The method"). A fix of a path or a section name is a change too. The writer's fixes of the cold read's flags land with no second cold read. Then the change lands without the curator's yes, also when you proposed it, unless the bullet after next says that it waits. A line of `references/sources.md` is not a rule, and needs neither a cold read nor a report.
- After a change to this skill or to `fortress-repo` lands, have a worker update that skill's page: the page of skill drafts or the page of `fortress-repo` changes, whose links the boot note holds (`references/skill-rewrite.md`, "The method", step 7). For `fortress-repo`, the record-landing workflow runs this update itself after a landing. The page of `fortress-repo` changes only shows the landed changes: it changes nothing in how that skill is updated. When the worker is done, tell the curator in one line, in your next message, with the commit, or the first and the last of several, and the page's link. Watch both pages for comments sent to Claude. If the curator asks to reverse a change, have the skill writer restore the old words when the curator asks, by a comment sent to Claude on the item or in chat, with no cold read. The reversal does not wait for the end of the curator's reading. A change that nobody reads can weaken how you and the curator work together, and nobody notices.
- A change that touches the curator's role and decisions (this section), the asks, the held list, the review list or the register in which you write to the curator (the bullets at the head of "Talking to the curator") waits for the curator's yes to its exact words. So does every rewrite of `SKILL.md` or of a whole part, since it can touch any rule. Put it as an item under "Proposed changes" on the page of skill drafts. Such a change has no default: it stays out of the skill until the yes. If you are unsure whether a change touches these, it waits.

1:# Running and reviewing a batch
32:## The go
38:## The workflow
47:## The roles
54:## The checker count and the distance
63:## Reserved points and repairs
71:## While it runs
79:## The landing

# Running and reviewing a batch

The batch workflow is `explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js` and its manual, `climb-batch-workflow.md` beside it. Its stages run in this order: the scatter of the rungs, the rung workers, the skeptics, the judges and the repair round, the gather, the merged-diff review, the gate, and the commit stage. Read a stage's section of the manual when you reach it: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md#<heading>'`.

**batch record**
: `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-<N>.md`, written by the planner before the launch. Its rung sections are the workers' briefs; its other sections are for the curator.

**base**
: Commit that the batch starts from.

**gather**
: Stage that merges the rungs and folds their reports and record lines into the tree.

**merged-diff review**
: Review of the gathered diff, beside the gate, of the records, the reserved points and the routing.

**repair round**
: One round of fixes after the merged-diff review or the gate.

**commit stage**
: Last stage, which commits the landed tree and runs the pass of `references/record.md`.

**reserved point**
: Point that a batch record keeps for the curator, such as a model or APL line beyond the approved ones, or an interpreter output that a rung cannot explain.

**checker count**
: Errors that the compiled checker reports on the interpreter's library, up to each component's first error.

**distance**
: All the compiled checker's errors on the interpreter's library, which must reach zero before the switch-over, the move of the compiled path onto the interpreter's library. The gate's distance stage counts them (`explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh`), and FACTS holds the current value.

## The go

- The batches of PLAN's phase 3 run on a standing go, in PLAN's order. Launch each when the batch before it has landed and its own batch record has no open question.
- If a question that the batch record raises is consequential (`SKILL.md`), put it to the curator first. Otherwise decide it and put it on the review list. While the curator is away, overnight, take its recommended default and put it on the review list. If that default would reverse a decision of the curator, hold that batch, and launch the repair batch (`explorations/coordinator/REPAIR-BATCH.md`) in its place.
- Have one Fable review read each coming batch record before the launch, with a go in advance. It is written for the curator in place of reading the record. Treat its questions as the batch record's.

## The workflow

- Between batches, improve the script and the manual where a batch showed a problem.
- Let every step spend the fewest workers that it needs.
- Build the base once, yourself, in a worktree where nobody compiles or runs (`args.baseBuild`). Every rung worktree is seeded from it (`explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh`), never built clean.
- No stage runs a build, a suite or a measurement again on a code state that another stage ran, and no agent reads again a log that has not changed.
- Let the planner give each rung its mission briefing, from the territory map (`explorations/coordinator/map/`), in neutral words: "the decisions on record", not the curator's name. Require no answers from the worker about how it searched.
- At each landing, report the share of briefed agents that read the briefing at all. Aim for all of them. By the brief's order, none reads it in its first turn.

## The roles

- The skeptic checks a rung's result after its worker, and builds nothing to check. It reads from the worker's transcript whether the test came first and failed. It runs its own small programs on the rung's build, and on the base through `explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh` with a private caches folder. Where the rung changes the compiled checker, the skeptic also runs the count stage itself, on the base build and on the worker's commits, as `fortress-repo`'s `compiler.md`, "The checker's time", gives a reviewer. That run is the one exception to this bullet and to the rule that no stage measures a code state again.
- It checks the result against the library's way, the ledger, sibling sites and the decisions on record, and fixes what it finds, test first.
- A judge rules only on a fix that the skeptic marks contested, on a rung that the skeptic refuses, or on a rung whose worker reported that it could not go on. The first ruling runs on Opus, a second on Fable (`judgeTier`). A settled fix lands with the review and the gate as its check. Reaching a reserved point, or a file outside what the rung's section of the batch record names, does not make a settled fix contested: it lands, and the point or the file goes on the review list. A point that cannot be undone holds the batch.
- No batch compares the printed outputs of the suites' test programs, and no baseline is run to compare against.

## The checker count and the distance

Until the switch-over lands, the gate of every batch reports the checker count and the distance. Neither turns the gate red.

- If a rung's test is the checker count or the distance, it takes the last landed gate's tables as its starting values.
- If every file that a rung changes lies outside what the two measures read, the rung runs neither and lists those files (`STAGE_BLIND`). Its skeptic checks the list against the branch's diff.
- The review after the batch ties every new or risen row of the count's table to a named rung edit.
- The gate's comparisons hide Java line numbers, identity hashes and moved library positions. Put every difference that they hid on the review list. Put there too each line of the team's tests that a rung rewrote to keep its checked value, with its before and after.

## Reserved points and repairs

- A reversible reserved point does not hold the batch. The batch lands with the point's default, and the point goes on the review list.
- An output that the base already varies from run to run, with the test's verdict unchanged, is a ledger row.
- After its one repair round, a merged-diff review that still blocks does not hold a batch whose gate is green. Its findings go on the review list, for the batch after. The review runs once in each batch.
- A repair after the gate runs the gate again only if it changes what the gate reads (its part in `fortress-repo`).
- If the gate over a merged batch is red, do not bisect. Find the cause as a whole, and rework that part in the merged batch. If the gate is still red after its repair, the batch does not land: put it to the curator at once, as a hold.

## While it runs

- At a boot, read the batch record's sections for the curator, the run's journal (`references/delegating.md`) at the run ID in the check-in file (below), and the times of its agents' transcripts in the session's `subagents/workflows/<run>/`.
- From the launch until the run ends, by landing, by stopping or by holding its push for the curator, edit no tracked file in the main tree, the boot note included. The gather needs `git status --porcelain` there to print nothing. Keep `origin/main` at or behind the main tree's head, or git refuses the commit stage's push. So push `main` from no other tree. From the main tree, push nothing that the batch committed: the commit stage pushes it.
- Before the launch, name the check-in file in the boot note: `<scratchpad>/batch<N>/checkins.txt`, where `<N>` is the batch's number. After the launch, write the run's ID and each armed check-in's ID in that file. If the scratchpad loses a check-in's ID, find the check-in again with `list_triggers`.
- Workers push to their own `wip/` branches as they go. A branch holds only what `main` is to hold (`fortress-repo`, its committing part).
- If a process stop or the usage limit ends the run, resume it (`references/delegating.md`). The limit drops no rung.

## The landing

The landing check is `ledger.py landing-check BASE`, run by the gather and by the merged-diff review on the batch's base. It reports a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test removed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status. A finding the base already had counts too. The gather clears each finding before its commit, through `rewrite`, `close` or `note`, or by a reworded entry. The merged-diff review clears any that is left in its corrections commit. So a batch lands only when the check prints nothing.

If the batch's push is held for the curator, take steps 1 to 3 at once on the local commits. Only these wait: the push, the parts of step 3's routing check that need the pushed hashes, and step 4, since the record-landing workflow pushes `main` itself. After the curator's go, push the batch yourself, by `fortress-repo`'s committing part. The review's commit of step 3 goes with that push. Then run step 4.

1. Sweep the batch agents' to-dos from the session's shared task list: `explorations/coordinator/tools/sweep-tasks.py --delete`. If another workflow still runs, add `--running`, which removes only the completed tasks. The agents write these to-dos themselves, and the harness shows the whole list to every agent.
2. Name each decision that landed in one line, and put the items for the curator on the review list.
3. Have one Opus reviewer, which only reads, check the landed changes against the decisions on record and the library's way; measure misses by kind, the briefing's use and cost, and re-measuring; and run the routing check (the manual, "After the landing: the coordinator's routing"). Have the review's section on cost count the tokens written in three spans, each on its own. Give the reviewer each span as two times, read from the commits and the workflow journals:

   - the landing work of the batch before: from its commit stage's last commit to the end of its record-landing workflow;
   - the preparation: from then to the launch of the batch under review;
   - the run: from that launch to its commit stage's last commit, which stands also while the push is held.

   Have the reviewer count a span as `spend.py` from its start less `spend.py` from its end, over the same folders. A transcript then counts in the span where it last changed.
4. After the post-batch review is committed, run the record-landing workflow (`explorations/coordinator/tools/record-landing/README.md`). It brings FACTS, POSITIONS, INDEX, PLAN and the review queue in line with the landing. Its Land stage, the step that lands its commits on `main`, also pushes them. Then it runs the orientation workflow in update mode itself, on the entries that the landing added or changed. The orientation workflow writes new text for each section of `fortress-repo`'s `revival-changes.md` that these entries touch. Next, the workflow has the skill writer install the sections that the orientation judge accepts. The writer also brings in line the sentences of `fortress-repo`'s other parts that the landing's changes to FACTS and POSITIONS made false, and no others. A new rule, or a change of a rule's meaning, is not made in the workflow: the writer lists it for you in its reports, `writer-1.md` and `writer-2.md` in `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/skills/`, and you put it to the curator as `references/skill-rewrite.md`, "The method", step 6, says. The workflow runs a cold read of the writer's changes, and the writer fixes its flags. Then it has a worker update the page of `fortress-repo` changes (`references/skill-rewrite.md`, "The method", step 7), and pushes the writer's commits, as its Land stage pushes the record's. No step of yours comes between. Its result gives one line with the commits and the page's link (the README, "The skill update"). If the landing made no sentence of the skill false and the orientation judge did not run, no writer starts, and the line names no page. While the workflow runs, start no skill-writer task of your own on `fortress-repo`.

   Then read the workflow's commits on `main`, as the README's "Landing its result" says. If the result's `stopped` is set, take the step that the README gives for it there: a stopped push leaves the commits on the local `main`, for you to push or take off. If the page agent could not publish, the line names the page's source: publish it yourself by the page's URL. File the orientation update's held sections, in its `queue.md`, in the review queue. Ask whether you would have done anything differently. Tell the curator of its POSITIONS changes as `SKILL.md`, "Quiet times", says. Send the curator the one line for the page of `fortress-repo` changes (`SKILL.md`, "The curator's role and decisions") when "Quiet times" allows: while the curator is away, hold it with the reports of skill changes. Once the reviews show the workflow sound, stop this review, and rely on what the workflow does.

18:## Which tier runs what
20:- Give each worker its tier's alias: `model: 'opus'`, `'sonnet'` or `'fable'`. Write no identifier that an alias resolves to.
28:- If you start a headless session on a tier other than Opus or Fable, set `FORTRESS_HEADLESS=1` in its environment. Otherwise the model check's alarm stops its work (`SKILL.md`, "The boot"). Today only the baseline interview does so.
53:- If you launch a long or large run outside a batch, such as a probe that builds and runs suites for an hour, write its estimate of tokens written in the boot note. A probe can write ten times its estimate.
54:- Watch its spend: `spend.py <since-epoch> <path>`, where the path is the session's `subagents/` folder for agents, or the project's folder for headless sessions. If it passes the estimate, give the worker an instruction or end it. Watch no other run this way.

\subsection{Comparisons Operators}

Unless otherwise noted, the operators described in this section
produce boolean (\VAR{true}/\VAR{false}) results.

The operators $<$, \EXP{\leq}, \EXP{\geq}, and $>$ are
  used for numerical comparisons
and are supported by integer, rational, and floating-point types.
Comparison of rational values throws \TYP{RationalComparisonError}
if either argument is the rational infinity \EXP{1/0} or the
rational indefinite \EXP{0/0}.
Comparison of floating-point values throws \TYP{FloatingComparisonError}
if either argument is a \TYP{NaN}.

The operators $<$, \EXP{\leq}, \EXP{\geq}, and \EXP{>} may also be
used to compare characters
(according to the numerical value of their Unicode codepoint values)
and strings (lexicographic order based on the character ordering).
They also use lexicographic order when used to compare lists
whose elements support these same comparison operators.
\Method*{\EXP{\KWD{opr} \mathord{=}(\KWD{self}, \VAR{other}\COLON \mathbb{Q})\COLON \TYP{Boolean}}}
\Method*{\EXP{\KWD{opr} \mathord{\geq}(\KWD{self}, \VAR{other}\COLON \mathbb{Q})\COLON \TYP{Boolean}}}
\Method*{\EXP{\KWD{opr} \mathord{>}(\KWD{self}, \VAR{other}\COLON \mathbb{Q})\COLON \TYP{Boolean}}}

The comparison operators \EXP{<}, \EXP{\leq}, \EXP{=}, \EXP{\geq}, and \EXP{>}
allow any rational value to be compared numerically to any other rational value.

The rational values are totally ordered except for \EXP{0/0},
which is unordered with respect to all other rational values;
moreover, for compatibility with floating-point arithmetic, \EXP{0/0} is
unordered with respect to itself, and therefore these five comparison operators
always return \VAR{false} if either argument is \EXP{0/0}.
The value \EXP{-\infty} is less than any finite rational value,
and \EXP{+\infty} is greater than any finite rational value.

object NaiveSeqGenerator[\E\](g: Generator[\E\])
        extends SequentialGenerator[\E\]
    getter size() = |g|
    getter asString():String = "naive seq(" g.asString ")"
    opr |self| : ZZ32 = |g|
    generate[\R\](r: Reduction[\R\], m:E->R): R = do
      rcompose(f:R->R, f':R->R): R->R = fn (x:R):R => f'(f(x))
      id(x:R):R = x
      mp(x:E):R->R = fn (a:R):R => r.join(a,m(x))
      f : R -> R = g.mapReduce[\R->R\](mp,rcompose,id)
      mt : R = r.empty()
      f mt
    end
end

trait RelationalPredicateCondition[\E\] extends { Condition[\()\] }
  relation() : (E, E) -> Boolean
  target() : Generator[\ E \]
  cond[\G\](t: () -> G, e: () -> G) : G = do
    (* println("condition is evaluated...") *)
    rel : (E, E) -> Boolean = relation()
    join(x : (Boolean, Maybe[\E\], Maybe[\E\]), y : (Boolean, Maybe[\E\], Maybe[\E\])) : (Boolean, Maybe[\E\], Maybe[\E\]) = do
      (b1, h1, l1) = x
      (b2, h2, l2) = y
      px : Boolean =
        if a <- l1 then
          if b <- h2 then rel(a, b) else true end
        else
          true
        end
      (b1 AND b2 AND px, if h1.holds then h1 else h2 end, if l2.holds then l2 else l1 end)
    end
    zero1 : (Boolean, Maybe[\E\], Maybe[\E\]) = (true, Nothing[\E\], Nothing[\E\])
    (res, h, l) = target().generate[\(Boolean, Maybe[\E\], Maybe[\E\])\](MapReduceReduction[\(Boolean, Maybe[\E\], Maybe[\E\])\](join, zero1), fn (v:E):(Boolean, Maybe[\E\], Maybe[\E\]) => (true, Just[\E\](v), Just[\E\](v)))
    if res then t() else e() end
  end
end

(* condition returned by relational predicate *)

  relation() : (E, E) -> Boolean = r

step(p: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], b: Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\]): (RR64, Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]) = do
    ids = corpus.tokens(b, 0); tg = corpus.tokens(b, 1); vm = corpus.valid(b); nv = SUM vm; pos = corpus.positions(b)
    (wte, wpe, lm, wq, wk, wv, wo, f1, f2) = (view(p, 0), view(p, 1), view(p, 2), view(p, 3), view(p, 4), view(p, 5), view(p, 6), view(p, 7), view(p, 8))
    h(m: Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = heads(m, blockSize, nHead, headDim)
    u(t: Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32,ZZ32)\]): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = unheads(t, nHead)
    (* -- forward, all (doc, pos) rows at once -- *)
    x = gather(wte, ids) + gather(wpe, pos); xp = rows(rmsn, x); x1 = rows(rmsn, xp)
    (q, k, v) = (x1 wq^T, x1 wk^T, x1 wv^T); (qh, kh, vh) = (h(q), h(k), h(v))
    a = rows(sm, mask + (qh kh^T) / SQRT (1.0 headDim)); hc = u(a vh)
    x2 = xp + hc wo^T; x3 = rows(rmsn, x2); m0 = x3 f1^T; mr = 0.0 MAX m0; x4 = x2 + mr f2^T

(* ------------------------------------------- L13-L28: STEP, one APL block.
   The three adapters vw h u are ordinary TYPED local functions, as C4:54-55
   are, because a name in APL text is a call of a typed host function now, not
   a push on a frame stack; a view of the flat vector, rank 4 and its inverse
   stay outside the sub-language.  Every statement ends in ⋄ : a line break does
   not separate two statements when the next line can continue the one above,
   and the program's strand names are exactly the ones that continue a line. *)
step(P: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\], b: Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\]): (RR64, Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]) = do
    vw(i: ZZ32): Array[\RR64,(ZZ32,ZZ32)\] = view(P, i)

# The base build, seeded worktrees and the old code

**seeding**
: Making a worktree with a copy of the build and caches of a built, clean worktree. `seed-worktree.sh` makes the copy and rewrites the paths in it (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").

**base build**
: Clean worktree at the base, built in place by ant, or seeded. Every other worktree is seeded from it.

**old code**
: Base's code, run from the base build with a private caches folder.

Once the base build is built, run its code only as "Running the old code" says, with a private caches folder outside it. Any other run writes into the caches that every worktree is seeded from.

## Finding or building a base build

- If your brief names a base build, use it.
- If not, look in `git worktree list`. Earlier base builds are at paths such as `/home/user/fortress-base<N>`. A worktree can be your base build if it passes three checks:
  - `git -C <it> rev-parse HEAD` prints your base;
  - `git -C <it> status --porcelain` prints nothing;
  - it holds `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`.
- If no worktree passes them, build one at a path of your own, outside the main tree. It takes about 200 s: start the build and the library order detached, with the `nohup` line of `session.md`, "Long commands". `<base-commit>` is your base: the commit that your brief names, else your tree's `HEAD` when you start. Say so in your report.

      git worktree add --detach <base-build> <base-commit>
      cd <base-build>          # then set up the call as build-and-caches.md says
      ant compileAll
      # then the library order (build-and-caches.md), then this walk run, which warms walk's caches:
      bin/fortress ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss
      git status --porcelain   # must print nothing: the seeding script refuses a base build that is not clean

If you check a fix against its old code, use a base build at the commit that the fix starts from. If a brief names the fix's base, the fix starts there. If not, the fix starts from `git merge-base <its branch> main`, or from the parent of its first commit on `main`.

## Seeding a worktree

A build, and a run of `bin/fortress` without a private caches folder, walk's too, write into the caches of the tree that they run in. So build and run only in a tree whose caches no other agent uses. Your brief says where you work. If your work builds or runs code and your brief gives you no tree of your own, seed a worktree of your own instead of building one. Then work only there.

Seeding takes about 3 s and 206 MB of disk. The new worktree runs walk and the compiled path right away, with the library already compiled.

    explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh <base-build> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]

- The script checks out `<branch>`: a local branch, else origin's, else a new branch cut from `<start-point>`, by default the base build's commit. With `-`, it makes a detached worktree at `<start-point>`.
- If the script exits 2, the base build is not built or not clean, and the script made nothing. Then make the worktree with `git worktree add`, build it yourself, and say so in your report.
- If the worktree already exists, the script keeps its branch. If it already has a build, the script keeps that too. `SEED_FORCE=1` replaces it.
- If you start in a worktree that has no build, seed it in place: name it as `<new-worktree>`, and its branch as `<branch>`.
- The script lists the library sources that differ from the base build's commit. Before a compiled run, take for each the step that `build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library", gives.
- If the script warns that the copied build is the base's, run `ant compileAll`, then the library order. Without the warning, `ant compileAll` keeps the seeded caches.
- If another agent seeded your worktree, make the script's two lists yourself: `git diff --name-only <base> -- Library ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin` for the library sources, and `git diff --name-only <base> -- ProjectFortress/src ProjectFortress/astgen build.xml` for the warning.
- Reuse another tree's build or caches only through this script.

## Running the old code

If your worktree holds an edit and you need the base's behaviour, run the old code instead of reverting your edit. For example, see a test fail, or compare a program's old and new output.

`old-fortress.sh` runs the base build's `bin/fortress`. It sets `FORTRESS_HOME` to the base build and `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the private caches folder that you name, over your settings. Name a folder inside your worktree's `tmp/`:

    OLD=explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss     # the compiled path ...
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P             # ... then the run
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss             # walk
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches junit <worktree>/ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/X.test [Y.test ...]   # compiled .test files, in one JVM

- Any copy of the tool works, because it runs the base build that its first argument names.
- On first use, it fills the private folder with a copy of the base build's caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). Later runs use the same folder.
- Every cache file that a run writes goes to the private folder, and nothing else that it writes under the base build stays. So several agents can run the old code at once.
- Keep your programs outside the base build too, because a program writes its own logs beside it. The tool refuses a private folder inside the base build (exit 2).

To run interpreter tests on the old code, run the base build's `harness-one.sh` with `FORTRESS_HOME` set to the base build:

    FORTRESS_HOME=<base-build> <base-build>/explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh \
        <worktree>/tmp/old-harness <worktree>/ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss

The `run` step of a compiled `.test` is a separate `bin/fortress run` process. It inherits `FORTRESS_HOME` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`, and takes its class path from `FORTRESS_CACHES`. If you compose a harness run by hand with `-Dfortress.caches=<folder>`, set `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the same folder. Otherwise the `run` step fails with "Could not load ... Resource not found".
# Setting up, building, the caches, and what to rebuild

**tree**
: Checkout of the repository: the main checkout or a worktree. In a command, `<tree>` is the tree that you work in: the one that your brief names, else the one that your session starts in.

**library order**
: Five compiles that build the compiled path's library into the caches.

**DSL grammar**
: `grammar` declaration in an api, which adds syntax for a domain-specific language.

**parser directory**
: New `fortress<random>rats` folder of 5.8 MB, in which a program that imports a DSL grammar gets a Rats! parser generated when it runs. The run makes it in its JVM's temporary directory and never deletes it.

## Setting up each call

Start every Bash call with these lines. They put you at the tree's root, where this skill's commands start unless they `cd`:

    cd <tree> && mkdir -p tmp
    export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH
    export FORTRESS_HOME=$PWD FORTRESS_THREADS=1 TMPDIR=$PWD/tmp JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"
    unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS

- If `/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64` or `ant` is missing, run `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y openjdk-25-jdk-headless ant` first.
- `bin/fortress` takes `FORTRESS_HOME` from the shell whenever it is set. If it names another tree, you run that tree's code. Check it with `echo $FORTRESS_HOME`.
- `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` is unset, because the proxy's trust-store flags in it break ant's JVM forks.

The lines give the settings of `explorations/experiment/env.sh`, with two differences:

- The JVM's temporary directory is your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- They leave out env.sh's removal of old parser directories in `/tmp`, because your runs put theirs in your tree's `tmp/` (below).

If your brief tells you to run `source env.sh` and then to point `TMPDIR` and `JAVA_FLAGS` at `tmp/`, use the lines above. They do the same.

The library and microGPT import no DSL grammar, and of the gated tests only `ProjectFortress/syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss` does. The ungated tests beside it import one, and so do the APL experiments under `explorations/apl/`.

With the lines above, your runs that import a DSL grammar put their parser directories in `<tree>/tmp/`. Hundreds of them once filled the disk allowance. So:

- When no run of yours is live, remove yours: `rm -rf <tree>/tmp/fortress*rats`.
- Before a long run, check `df -h /`. How to read it: the `cloud-container` skill.

\revision{revival-overloading}{This section is new.
The Working Draft of February 2011 required overloaded declarations to have
identical static parameters and ignored them.
The rules stated are those of the type group's paper of 2011 (Allen, Hilburn,
Kilpatrick, Luchangco, Ryu, Chase, and Steele, ``Type Checking Modular Multiple
Dispatch with Parametric Polymorphism and Multiple Inheritance'', OOPSLA 2011),
which the compiled type checker applies, with its Return Type Rule checked over
every instance of the less specific declaration; the pair refused above has the
shape of that paper's own example, which the compiled path used to accept and
then fail to verify.
The interpreter runs the pair allowed above, reading two declarations with
static parameters on their declared domains, each over its own instances, where
no pair of their parameter types excludes each other; the compiled code
generator fails on it (row~537 of the revival's gap ledger).
The compiled implementation adds one restriction that is not a rule of the
language.
When one declaration with static parameters is more specific than another that
declares as many static parameters of its own, the two must declare them of the
same kinds, position by position, and the return type of the more specific one
must be a subtype of the other's when their static parameters are identified
position by position; for its code generator hands the static arguments that a call writes,
by position, to whichever declaration the call dispatches to (row~398 of the
revival's gap ledger).

the other order, where \TYP{Pr} is an object with two type parameters:
%trait Maker

%end
%object M extends Maker
%  make[\A, B\](): Pr[\B, A\] = Pr[\B, A\](1)
%end

73:## The library order
74-
75-The first of its compiles, `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, holds the top type `Any`, which both libraries share. The other four are the compiler's own. All five take about 100 to 110 s after `ant compileAll`.
76-
77-Run it only when the caches lack the library's jars, or hold stale ones:
78-
79-- after a build that printed `Caches <tree>/default_repository/caches started again, empty`, and in a tree whose caches are empty;
80-- after an edit of a library `.fsi` that the section "After an edit of the library" names.
81-
82-Otherwise the jars are in place, and a compiled test or program needs no library order. The five commands:
83-
84-    cd ProjectFortress
85-    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss            # 17 s
#!/bin/bash
# codegen.sh <out-dir>: the code generator over the one library's components, declaration by declaration, on the
# tree at $FORTRESS_HOME (climb batch 25's planner), made from the probe of 2026-10-23
# (perf-probes/codegen-distance/REPORT.md, sections 1 and 3, whose run.sh and classify2.py were not kept): the
# distance stage's own shadows, made from the tracked sources at this run (tools/distance/shadow-patch.py and
# add-patch.py), and its driver, DistanceMulti, run with -order full (every compiler phase, code generation among
# them) and -setting compile, the compile command's own setting, which the distance stage runs (its run.sh), over
# the stage's fourteen components in its order. The report's flags: -Dprobe.tolerant=true (the checker checks each
# declaration apart and its errors stop nothing; code generation catches each declaration's failure),
# -Dprobe.bottomCompare=true, -Dprobe.skipOverloads=true (no dispatch methods), the overloading memo off.
# Writes <out-dir>/run.txt and prints the classified table (cgkinds.py). One JVM, -Xmx4g; about 200 s on an idle box.
set -u
O=$(mkdir -p "$1" && cd "$1" && pwd)
FH=${FORTRESS_HOME:-$PWD}
D="$FH/explorations/coordinator/tools/distance"
HERE=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)
COMPONENTS="Library/FortressLibrary.fss Library/RangeInternals.fss ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss
 ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/NativeArray.fss Library/List.fss Library/String.fss Library/FlatString.fss Library/Stream.fss
 ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/NatReflect.fss Library/TypeProxy.fss Library/Writer.fss ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss
 Library/CovariantCollection.fss Library/OneShotFlag.fss"
rm -rf "$O/shadow-src" "$O/shadow-classes" "$O/classes" "$O/caches" "$O/tmp"
mkdir -p "$O/shadow-src" "$O/shadow-classes" "$O/classes" "$O/caches" "$O/tmp"
CP=$("$FH/bin/fortress_classpath" 2>/dev/null | tail -1 | sed 's#:[^:]*/default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache##')
( cd "$FH" && python3 "$D/shadow-patch.py" ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress "$O/shadow-src" \
           && python3 "$D/add-patch.py" "$O/shadow-src" ) > "$O/shadows.txt" 2>&1 || { echo "shadows stale"; exit 1; }
javac -nowarn -encoding UTF-8 -cp "$CP" -d "$O/shadow-classes" \
    "$O/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java" \
    "$O/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/phases/TypeCheckPhase.java" \
    "$O/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/phases/DesugarPhase.java" \
    "$O/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/phases/CodeGenerationPhase.java" \
    "$O/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java" \
    "$O/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/Desugarer.java" \
    "$O/shadow-src/com/sun/fortress/nodes_util/NodeComparator.java" >> "$O/shadows.txt" 2>&1 || { echo "shadows do not compile"; exit 1; }
javac -nowarn -cp "$CP" -d "$O/classes" "$D/DistanceMulti.java" >> "$O/shadows.txt" 2>&1 || exit 1
S=$(date +%s)
( cd "$FH" && timeout -k 30 5400 java -Xmx4g -Xss64m -XX:-OmitStackTraceInFastThrow \
      -Djava.io.tmpdir="$O/tmp" -Dfortress.caches="$O/caches" \
      -Dprobe.tolerant=true -Dprobe.bottomCompare=true -Dprobe.skipOverloads=true -Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=false \

So walk checks no static types of expressions: an ill-typed expression shows only when it runs, as a failed dispatch or as another run-time error, such as F-239's refusal of an `if` on a value that is not a `Boolean`. At load, walk refuses some ill-formed declarations: the `fortress-repo` skill's `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists them, with their evidence in F-29 (`comprises` clauses), F-142 (the Meet Rule for Functional Methods) and F-145 (uncovered abstract methods and `override`). The phases and where the two paths part: the skill's "How a program runs". Detail: `explorations/repo-internals.md`, "The two worlds".
8	- F-9 **`fortress typecheck` checks a program against the compiler's library, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`, so it is no oracle for walk programs.** `Shell.java` calls `useCompilerLibraries()` for the command (row 69). P-12 has walk run the checker on its own programs after the switch-over, and walk cannot do so as it stands: it runs with type checking and the Scala checker off, the Java checker is gone (`compiler/StaticChecker.java:228-229`), and it has no case for the `CoercionInvocation` nodes that the checker inserts, by reading (row 833).
9	- F-11 **The code generator boxes every number, and boxing is the main representational cost of microGPT-shaped array code.** So a compiled `RR64` loop holds no `dadd` or `dmul` (the `fortress-repo` skill, "The compiled run time"). In Java models of microGPT's three kernels, boxed elements cost 6.3× (dot product), 6.5× (matrix product) and 2.6× (row lift) over `double[]`. No such kernel compiles yet: the compiler prelude has no array type (row 305), and the arrays reach the compiled path with the one library (P-37). In a hot compiled loop, escape analysis removes the temporary boxes, and one box per assignment to a mutable variable per iteration stays (F-301), as long as C2's inline depth reaches each box's constructor chain (F-302). Detail: `perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md` sections 2 and 4; `perf-probes/helper-calls/REPORT.md` section 4.
10	- F-12 **On the compiled path, the scalar `RR64` loop `bench1t` ran in 0.74 s in one session's measurement; the loop still pays for its generator, for boxing and for a transaction check at each use of its accumulator.** `bench1t` is `for i <- seq(1#20000000) do acc := acc 0.9999999 + 0.0000001 end` on a `var acc: RR64`, with both literals written in the loop. The time is the median of three loop-only runs at one thread (`compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`, "The four timings"). Times taken in different sessions differ on this machine, so compare only times from one session. What the loop does, read in its bytecode (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` sections 4 and 5): the `seq` loop becomes the compiler prelude's `countedseqloop`, which runs the iterations in order by a recursive split over boxed indices, with a closure call per element; each value is boxed (F-11); and the accumulator is a volatile cell whose read and write each first call `BaseTask.inATransaction`, as for every mutable local (F-40, what a size costs at run time, whose sized loop pays the same check). Within the boxing and the cell, the report counts four allocations per iteration, an interface call to the native wrapper and the casts, the part that unboxed doubles and `double[]` would attack. No share of the 0.74 s is measured.
11	- F-17 **The bytecode cache can come up empty after a library order that reports exit 0.** Running the same commands again, one at a time, made the jars. The cause is not known. Check the five jars before a compiled run (the `fortress-repo` skill's `build-and-caches.md`, "The library order"). Detail: `perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md` section 1.
12	- F-18 **On the compiled path, the class loader makes the class of a generic instantiation at its first use, by rewriting the template's bytecode with ASM, and the rewriting only renames, so it gives no instance a `double[]` field.** The class is `InstantiatingClassloader`; the `fortress-repo` skill's "The compiled run time" gives the mechanism. A size is part of the made class's name, as in `pNatMeth$Box⟦3⟧`, the object `Box` at size 3 in the probe component `pNatMeth`. Inside the class, the size's descriptor is `RTTIsize.of("<n>")` (F-129). A field of the template's type `T`, `LT;`, becomes `LFRR64;` in `Box⟦FRR64⟧`, and `[D` is no class name, so stamping alone keeps every number boxed (F-11). Detail: `perf-probes/nat/java.md` section 1; `coordinator/array-design.md` section 2 (probe 1); `reviews/array-design-ways.md` section 3, way A4.

For the elements of a tuple and the operands of an operator, each path starts a task only where it judges it worth it: walk by `TupleTask.worthSpawning`, which also governs a call's arguments, and the code generator by `ParallelismAnalyzer`. Compiled, a function call's arguments run in order (`CodeGen.evalArg`). A `for` loop over a range without `seq` runs by splitting the range into `do … also do … end` blocks. Under walk, every such block is a task, and walk's library splits down to single elements (`Library/RangeInternals.fss`). Compiled, the first block runs in place, and each other block forks only where `BaseTask.forkIfProfitable` judges it worth it, as tuple elements do; the compiler prelude's `parloop` splits down to `FORTRESS_LOOP_CHUNK` elements, 1 by default. `FORTRESS_THREADS` sizes the pool of worker threads (the `fortress-repo` skill, "Parallelism and mutable state"). By grep, no program under `explorations/`, the model programs and the probes, writes `spawn`, which starts an explicit thread, or an `also do` block, so their parallelism comes only from loops, tuples and arguments. The array-type syntax `T[n]` with a `nat` parameter does not unify with such an array, "Cannot unify … with ArrayType", where `T[3]` with a literal size does (row 23). Walk matches sizes at dispatch. A mismatch, such as a `DOT`, the library's inner product, of a 2×3 matrix by a 2×3 matrix, whose inner sizes differ, is a `ProgramError`, "Failed to find any matching overload", that no `catch` takes (row 254). 15	- F-21 **The February 2011 Working Draft's bare `Nothing`, one object for every `T`, is accepted on neither path: the grammar refuses its `excludes` clause, and without that clause `T` is undefined.** The declaration is `object Nothing extends Maybe[\T\] excludes Just[\T\] where {T extends Object}` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/convenience.tex:40`). 16	- F-22 **When a component's name differs from the api that it exports, neither path finds the component, for an exported function or variable alike.** The specification resolves an imported api to any component that exports it (`Specification/basic/components/overview.tex`). The tree looks only under the api's name, unless a user maps the api to its component by hand with `LinkShell`'s `alink` or `clink`. The linker's component repository looks this way (`Linker.whoIsImplementingMyAPI`), so `fortress link` and walk print "Could not find an implementation for API … on path" before any code is generated. The code generator names a reference to an exported declaration after the api, and the declaring class after the component. The link step rewrites such a reference to the component only when the repository names it, so files compiled one by one, without `fortress link`, die with `NoClassDefFoundError`. The missing step is the repository's: finding the component that exports the api. The report names two repairs, neither built: the repository could search the source path for that component, or the code generator could emit api-named forwarders, for which three comments in `CodeGen.java` leave a place. Walk and `fortress link` need the first. Workaround: name the api after its component. Gated by the expected failure `compiler_tests/XXXExportVarRungXLinked.test` (row 320). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-export-var/REPORT.md`, "The measurement that separates them".

Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/REPORT.md` section 6, D1.
18	- F-24 **Under `walk`, a native can raise a Fortress exception that a Fortress `catch` sees.** It throws a `FortressError` that holds the exception's object, as `Int.overflow()` does for `IntegerOverflow` (F-132; row 347, fixed). Gated by the `overflows(...)` assertions of `tests/IntSemanticsRungI.fss`, and for a helper by `tests/NativeHelperRaiseWalk.fss` and, for each of the five types, `tests/<type>DivisionByZeroWalk.fss` and `tests/<type>RemainderByZeroWalk.fss`. 19	- F-25 **On the compiled path, the class loader loads each class under the JDK's class-loading lock, so the first load of an instantiation's class is safe on four threads at once.** `InstantiatingClassloader.loadClass` holds `getClassLoadingLock(name)` for the whole load, as the JDK's own `ClassLoader.loadClass` does. Without the lock, two threads that first loaded such classes at the same time could race, and the run died with a `NullPointerException` (row 417, fixed). The test `compiler_tests/FirstLoadThreadsRungG` calls the generic overload `f[\T\](v: Vt[\T\])` at eight instantiations, `Vt[\A1\]` to `Vt[\A8\]`, from a parallel `for` loop of 800 iterations. Observed: at four threads it failed 5 runs of 5 before the lock, and passed 5 of 5 after. It is one of the gate's atomic runs, which run each program at four threads (`gate.md`). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/REPORT.md` sections 1 (the runs) and 12 (why this lock).
20	- F-26 **Under walk, when one of two applicable declarations has static parameters of its own, the call chooses on their declared domains where exactly one lies inside the other, not by the order in which they are written.** It builds P-45, the choice among overloads by declared parameter types, under walk. A declaration has static parameters of its own if it is a generic function or constructor, or a functional method with static parameters in a trait or object without any. Its declared domain, walk's symbolic instance, is its parameter types with each type parameter standing for itself under its bounds. Where neither declared domain lies inside the other, where each lies inside the other, or where neither declaration has static parameters of its own, walk compares the domains of the instances that the call makes. So a functional method of a generic trait or object is compared on its instance, and a generic dotted method is chosen by F-253 (a generic method at a dotted call, also chosen on declared domains). If the chosen declaration is generic and its instance takes an argument only by a conversion, walk converts the argument and dispatches the converted arguments again, so the most specific declaration for the converted values runs. In two cases walk keeps the chosen instance, with no second dispatch: an overloaded dotted method, and a position whose conversion `Coercions.coercionFor` does not find, such as a tuple converted element by element. Two generic overloads whose static parameters agree in name, kind and bounds share one symbolic instance, even if their `where` clauses differ; no test or library declaration has such a pair (row 478). Gated by `tests/DispatchDeclaredDomain.fss` and `DispatchConvertedAgain.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-dispatch/REPORT.md` sections 5.1, 5.2 (the second dispatch) and 5.5 (the symbolic instance).
21	- F-27 **Walk's load check reads again two kinds of overload pair that its parameter-by-parameter check refuses, and accepts those that pass: a generic declaration beside a plain one, read on their declared domains, and two plain top-level functions, not methods, whose overlap other declarations cover through `comprises` clauses.** To test a cover, the check cuts the overlap of the two domains, position by position, into parts by the `comprises` clauses. Each combination of parts must lie inside the domain of one declaration without static parameters that lies below both. So several such declarations may together cover the overlap. A search that does not settle refuses. A generic declaration beside a plain one passes where one declared domain lies strictly inside the other and the inner one's return type lies below the outer one's. Where neither lies inside the other, the pair needs the same cover, or declared domains that exclude each other read whole (F-258, exclusion over the whole parameter type). Equal declared domains are refused. It builds under walk P-46, by which a conversion never changes which declaration runs when one already fits, and P-60, by which several declarations below both may cover a meet. Two generic declarations are read on their declared domains too (F-252: the No Duplicates, Return Type and Meet Rules, each over its own instances). Walk still refuses the valid example of the POPL 2019 paper on symmetric multiple dispatch (`research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md`, p. 11:13), a set of three generic declarations (row 539). Gated by `tests/ComprisesMeetWalk.fss` and `GenericBesidePlain*.fss`, among others. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-dispatch/REPORT.md` sections 5.3 (generic beside plain) and 5.4 (the cover).
22	- F-28 **Walk instantiates a generic declaration declared to return `Any`.** `MakeInferenceSpecific` treats `Any` as it treats a trait type (row 157, fixed). Its visitor has no case for 11 of the syntax tree's 18 concrete type classes, and of those only the dimension forms can be written as a return type. Gated by `tests/GenericReturningAny.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-dispatch/REPORT.md` section 3.
23	- F-29 **Under walk, the load check refuses a trait or object that extends a closed trait of the program's main component where the trait's `comprises` clause does not allow it.** A closed trait is one with a `comprises` clause. The check reads every trait and object of every component of the program, the library's included, as a possible extender. An extender is allowed in three cases: it lies below a listed type; it is a trait whose own `comprises` clause lists only types that are allowed in turn; or it is a generic trait that some trait or object extends, and each of those extenders lies below a listed type (`Specification/basic/traits.tex`, "Trait Declarations"). The check does not yet read a clause declared outside the main component, the library's among them (row 551), or an object expression's `extends` clause (row 597). Nor does it check that each listed type extends the trait at every instantiation (row 598). A check that read the library's clauses would refuse at load every program that imports the library's `Reflect` (row 595), and four team tests and two demos whose objects extend `Number` or `Exception` directly (row 596). Their repairs come before that check and are the curator's. Gated by `tests/ComprisesUnlistedExtender` and `ComprisesGenericChildUnlistedExtender`, refused at load, and by the `XXX` tests of rows 487 (a type of another component below a generic subtrait of a closed trait), 551, 597 and 598, which stay green while walk still loads their programs. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-load-check/REPORT.md` section 5.
24	- F-269 **Under walk, a program's declarations of a library operator name are checked against the library's only when the program declares two or more of that name, and only on a cold cache.** One such declaration is not checked. Two or more are checked with the library's declarations, and the check can refuse them beside the library's generic declarations, even where they are more specific than the library's. It refused C4's former pair of `MAX` between an `RR64` and an `Array[\RR64,I\]`, in both orders, which C4 dropped when F-119's scalar extension took its place (row 341). It refuses the `Matrix`-specialised elementwise `×` of `apl/mg/elemwise_nat_probe.fss` (F-155). Walk writes a component to its cache before it runs this check, and skips the check on a component that it reads back. So a refusal appears once, on a cold cache, and never again (row 342). The check runs only when walk analyses the library itself again: deleting the program's own cache entries does not bring it back (row 342). So a test that depends on this check must run from an empty cache. Detail: rows 341 and 342; `compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/REPORT.md` section 4, a gated run that met a warm cache.
25	- F-291 **With the bound `Any`, the compiled path compiles, loads and runs generics at tuple and arrow static arguments as it does with `extends Any` written; `()` fails whatever the bound (row 339), and so does a generic dotted method with one tuple-typed parameter (row 832).** Measured once: generic functions, objects and traits, dispatch to a generic arm and `typecase`, at a pair or an arrow, with the static argument written or inferred. The class loader made the same classes by name, and the program jars read the same under `javap`, as the same programs with `extends Any` written under the compile command's bound `Object`. So the switch to the bound `Any` costs the run time no work for these shapes; its test cost is F-292. Not run: the one library's own instantiations at tuples, tuples of three or more and nested ones, generic functional methods at a tuple, a native that receives a tuple. With `extends Object` written, they are refused, or pass unchecked where the static argument is written (row 470); the compile command's bound is `Any` (`Shell.java:372`). No gated test. Detail: `perf-probes/bound-any-compiled/REPORT.md`, "The shapes by setting" and "What the class loader makes".
26	- F-301 **On the compiled path a native helper is called through a generated wrapper over the box classes, and once the loop is hot C2 inlines the whole path, so the call costs nothing of its own.** A binding `builtinPrimitive("pkg.Class.method")` and a written `import java` alias call compile to the same bytes: an `invokestatic` of `native.pkg.Class.method`, a class the compiled path writes into `nativewrapper_cache/`, which unboxes each argument with `getValue`, calls the helper and boxes its result with `make`, a new box each time (`compiler/nativeInterface/FortressMethodAdapter.java:303-327`; `compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32.java:22-24`). A functional method such as `ZZ32`'s `+` reaches the wrapper through the dispatcher, an interface call, the springboard and the trait's static body. C2 inlines all of these frames, the helper, `make` and the box's constructor chain; only C1's profiling code refuses the helper and the chain's deep frames. Escape analysis then removes every temporary box, a helper's result passed into another helper among them, and one box stays per assignment to a mutable variable per iteration: 16 bytes for a `ZZ32`, 24 for an `RR64`. The library's form and the prelude's allocate the same. Observed once on one small program, `perf-probes/helper-calls/HelperCalls.fss`, by `javap`, C2's inlining log and the bytes that JFR counted, with no timing, on a machine shared at a load of 20 to 25; no test checks it. Detail: `perf-probes/helper-calls/REPORT.md` sections 2 to 5.
27	- F-302 **In those loops C2 inlines down to depth 12 from the loop, against the 16 at which it stops by default, and a temporary box whose constructor chain passes the limit is no longer removed.** At JDK 25's default `MaxInlineLevel=15` a frame at depth d inlines when d is at most 16. So an operator called from more than 4 further inlined frames keeps its temporary boxes. If `FZZ32` extends the one library's springboard after the switch-over, the margin is 2 frames; not measured, since nothing compiles against the one library yet. Observed once (F-301). Detail: `perf-probes/helper-calls/REPORT.md` sections 3 and 4.

30	- F-32 **The compiled path cannot reuse walk's glue classes, the Java classes that 161 of the one library's 449 live native bindings still name.** A native binding is a library body `builtinPrimitive("…")`; its string names a glue class, which takes walk's boxed values, or a static helper of `nativeHelpers/`, over plain Java values, which both paths call (F-298; F-299 holds the 288 that name one). MicroGPT's `nanoTime` names a helper (F-314); it also needs `getProgramArgsPrim`, which `System` calls as it loads; and `NativeArray`. The last two have no compiled analogue. The 42 with no analogue: `NativeArray` waits for the array decision on how a float vector's `double[]` store goes (P-85), and `Thread`, `Reflect` and `printTaskTrace` are off microGPT's path. Detail: `perf-probes/prelude/natives-shape.md` section 2; `coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-23.md`, section 4, "The planner's probes", "On the new base" and "The count".
